utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the appearances now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues Ms. McHenry, Mr. Turone and Mr. Khan for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is your application on notice to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I wish to make an application this morning, your Honour, for a subpoena to be issued. I understand it has been served, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have appearances for the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic and Mr. Zejnil Delalic is co-defended by my colleague Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am Zeljko Olujic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zdravko Mucic. I am an attorney from Zagreb, Croatia. Together with me, Mr. Mucic is co-defended by Mr. Michael Greaves, attorney from the United Kingdom and Northern Ireland.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, Defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic, and I am assisted by my co-counsel, Mr. Thomas Moran from Houston Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. Mr. Esad Landzo is represented here this morning by Cynthia McMurrey and by me; my name is John Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please. Your Honours, yesterday there was filed with the Registry by the Office of the Prosecutor a request by the Prosecutor for the issuance of a subpoena ad testificandum and an order to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina in relation to the compliance with those subpoenas. Your Honours, I have prepared submissions to assist you in relation to the law of this matter, having regard to the history of subpoenas in this jurisdiction, and I will go through these submissions if that is of assistance to your Honours in relation to the matter. Firstly, your Honour, the reason why these subpoenas are now sought is because of a failure and breakdown in the liaison efforts by the Office of the Prosecutor in order to secure the attendance of the persons mentioned in the subpoena. These things, your Honours, do change, so it may be that co-operation may be forthcoming now that the step has been taken for us to seek from your Honours a subpoena to issue. Your Honours, I have outlined yesterday and the -- I should say the day before, the considerable importance that the Prosecution attaches to the evidence that these witnesses can provide to the Tribunal in order to assist your Honours in the determination of the guilt or innocence of the accused in this case. The application before your Honours is in two parts, the first part being a subpoena ad testificandum against various individuals therein mentioned and an order against the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Just dealing briefly, your Honours, with the question of your Honours' powers concerning a subpoena against an individual, and the basis upon which it is our submission your Honours are permitted to issue such a subpoena, it is firstly necessary for your Honours to look briefly at Article 6 of the Statute of the Tribunal, which gives the jurisdiction -- which gives the Tribunal jurisdiction over natural persons, so that is the first step, in our submission, which goes towards the authority vested in this Trial Chamber to make the order sought. The second and very important article, your Honours, in the foundation of this authority, is Article 8. Article 8 in the Statute of the Tribunal is very broad and very encompassing. It provides that the Tribunal shall have territorial jurisdiction which: "... shall extend to the territory of the Former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, including its land surface, airspace and territorial waters. The temporal jurisdiction of the International Tribunal shall extend to a period beginning on 1 January 1991." Your Honours, that is a very broad conferral of jurisdiction on the Tribunal, and in many ways it equates the authority on the territory on the former Yugoslavia to that of a national court in that jurisdiction, in that it has jurisdiction on the land surface in relation to things upon the land surface -- in our submission, including individuals. This equation to a national court is in our submission further reinforced by Article 9, which provides that the Tribunal and national courts have concurrent jurisdiction to prosecute, and in particular, Article 9(2), which says: "The International Tribunal shall have primacy over national courts", in relation to matters which fall within the jurisdiction of this Tribunal. So, your Honours, we have those two very significant provisions in the Statute in relation to the powers of the Tribunal to issue a subpoena, and to issue a subpoena particularly to someone on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and I should say, your Honours, that all these persons that are sought to be brought to the Tribunal by way of subpoena are on the territory of the former Yugoslavia. Your Honours, in addition to the Statute there is in the Rules Rule 54, which provides that the Trial Chamber may issue such orders, summonses, subpoenas, warrants and transfer orders as may be necessary. So here, your Honour, there is contained in the rule an express mention of the word "subpoena". In terms, your Honour, of the Tribunal exercising powers over individuals, which is really in effect what a subpoena is, there are other rules which are -- which purport to exercise control over individuals, and firstly Rule 39, in particular Rule 39(i), gives the power to the Prosecutor to summons and question suspects, victims and witnesses and then, in paragraph (iv), empowers the judges to make orders as may be necessary arising under that provision. Further, your Honours, in Rule 77(C), there is an express reference to any person, it says -- this is the rule that deals with contempt, your Honours may recall, and the contempt provision deals mostly with witnesses and so forth that appear before the Tribunal, but paragraph (C) is much broader than just witnesses and purports to deal with: "Any person who attempts to interfere with or intimidate a witness." In our submission, this is a further illustration of the width of the rules in terms of dealing with individuals. Rule 90bis, which relates to the transfer of detained persons, is another example of a rule which permits an individual to be dealt with by way of direct order of the Tribunal, and finally your Honours, in relation to the Tribunal exercising powers over individuals, there is Rule 98, and Rule 98 deals with the power of the Chamber to order production of additional evidence, and the second sentence of Rule 98 expressly states that it may itself summons witnesses and order their attendance. In our submission, that is a clear indication, particularly the reference to order their attendance, of this Tribunal having the power by the Rules and by the Statute to exercise control over individuals. As your Honours are no doubt aware, this matter has been examined by the Trial Chamber II in the case of Blaskic, where a request for a subpoena has been made, and -- I correct myself here, your Honour, it has been considered in the Blaskic case, as opposed to in the Blaskic Chamber. In that decision the question of the Tribunal's power to issue subpoenas was considered, and it was decided in that case that the absence of any express power does not negate the existence of an implied power. But I would submit, your Honour, that there is an express power; the express power appears in Rule 54, and that express power is reinforced by other rules, and in particular by the Statute, which invests personal and territorial jurisdiction in the former Yugoslavia in this Tribunal. So it was concluded in that decision that the power did exist. So, your Honours, in our submission the authority to issue such a subpoena in circumstances that I have outlined here, that is in this case where you are dealing with individuals located on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, it is our submission that, based with the decision in the Blaskic case relating to subpoenas, there is no question of your Honours' authority to issue this subpoena. Turning, your Honours, to the second order which is sought, which is the order against the BiH, this is a much more straightforward provision, in our submission. It arises directly from Article 29 of the Statute, and in particular, Article 29(2)(b). It provides that: "States shall comply without undue delay with any request for assistance or", in this case, "an order issued by a Trial Chamber, including, but not limited to". Then (b): "The taking of testimony and the production of evidence." In our submission, your Honour, that clearly sets forth the power that this Chamber has to send an order accompanying this subpoena to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Again, your Honours, this matter has been examined in the decision on a subpoena in the Blaskic case, and based on Article 29(2)(b), the judge in that case determined that power to issue an order accompanying a subpoena is clearly provided for. Your Honours, there are, in various national jurisdictions that deal with implementing of orders of this Tribunal that have been enacted by the various states, examples of where those states have, by virtue of their legislation and co-operation, provided specifically for persons to be made available to come forward and give evidence and to produce articles before the Tribunal in the course of any proceedings, subject to an order of the International Tribunal, and in particular the various versions of this, and I will not trouble to go through them all in detail, but the various versions of this can be seen in German legislation, Spanish law and New Zealand legislation and also under the provisions of the United Kingdom. So there are, your Honours, examples of that in the national implementing legislation that where orders in the nature of an order issued under 29(2)(b) will be complied with in order to secure the attendance or produce the evidence of a witness. Your Honours, finally, we have the position of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina itself. I have said that our efforts to secure the attendance of these persons before the Chamber have been unsuccessful, and that our negotiations in this respect have broken down in the achievement of this. I should say, and hasten to say, that that is not as a consequence of any lack of will by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina as such. It does relate to the individuals themselves. One could argue, I suppose, that people could always go further in providing co-operation, but the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina has been co-operative. It is a difficult matter, because of the seniority of some of the people that we are seeking to call, but I should say that they have previously indicated their willingness to co-operate with the Tribunal in terms of a subpoena, the subpoena in the Blaskic case. Their officials have told us in this indication that they will comply with an order to ensure that these persons are brought to the Tribunal. I say that, and I say that they may be unsuccessful, just as in any national jurisdiction one may endeavour to do something, but not succeed. There is always the possibility they will not succeed, but they have indicated that they will co-operate and will comply with the order, should your Honours be disposed to issue one. So, your Honours, in conclusion, it is my submission that there is ample power in your Honours to issue this subpoena. The subpoena is essential in order to secure the attendance of these persons, and their evidence is very important for the Prosecution case, and, in my submission, the co-operation promised by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina is a further factor which we would use as a basis to urge your Honours to issue the subpoenas in this case. The subpoenas are necessary now, unfortunately, and I regret that we have had to bring it on with such urgency, but unfortunately we were optimistic that we would be able to achieve co-operation, but we were brought to this point when it became clear that we could not secure the attendance of these persons by any other means. So our submission, your Honours, is that your Honours do have the power and it is an appropriate matter and we seek your Honours' order so that subpoenas may be issued in relation to these named individuals. As your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Niemann. I am a little worried. In view of the clear words of Rule 54, why did you prefer to come to the Trial Chamber? Why could you not have gone to a judge?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it occurred to us that it may be better not to deal with this matter ex parte. I think, your Honours, that Rule 54 clearly gives your Honours the authority to do it, because it expressly mentions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I agree, it is in the alternative.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The other reason for it, your Honours, is that we are seeking an order under Rule 29 of the articles, and under Article 29, I will just go to it if I may, Article 29 expressly provides that under Article 29(2) that: "States shall comply without undue delay with any request for assistance or an order issued by a Trial Chamber." It uses the words "Trial Chamber". That is to be contrasted, your Honours, with Article 18(4), which provides that upon determination that a prima facie case exists, the Prosecution shall prepare -- I am sorry. Excuse me a moment. (Pause). Sorry, your Honours. Article 19(2). Article 29(2) is, in my submission, to be contrasted with Article 19(2), which gives a similar power to a judge to issue orders, arrest, detention, surrender and so forth relating to the conduct of the trial, but an order under paragraph 2 of Article 19 would not have the same force and effect as an order Article 29, paragraph 2, which expressly makes reference to the Trial Chamber. I would venture to suggest, your Honours, that the difference between Article 19(2) and Article 29(2) is grounded in the fact that Article 29(2) is a very powerful provision and it relates to the Tribunal making orders binding upon a state. That is a very serious step to be taken, and I venture to suggest that the drafters of the Statute considered that such a serious step should not be taken unless it was taken by a Trial Chamber as opposed to a judge. I may be wrong in that, but that is what I consider may be the difference between the two. But we are expressly seeking an order under 29(2), and that can only be done by a Trial Chamber. It seems to us, your Honour, that the appropriate Trial Chamber is this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do agree that there should be an order if there is any good reason for an order against any party who without an order would not comply with the direction. That is perhaps my view about it. Then in that case, one should be able to show why an order is necessary in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Especially against the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think it would be unfair of me to say that the failure of these people to attend rests entirely on the state. I do not think that is true at all. I think the individuals are largely responsible, but what I am saying is that the state, if given an order under 29(2) have led us to believe that they will comply with that order, the state in this case will comply with the order and give effect to the subpoena. The subpoena itself, of course, is directed to the individuals, so it is a two stage process. It is our belief that such an order would be successful in terms of the state complying with it. It is not as though we hold any apprehension that the state is simply going to ignore the order of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have any reaction from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: My learned friend need not apologise for seeking these orders urgently. As someone who prosecutes and defends in the United Kingdom, my experience is they are frequently orders which are sought urgently. One has no views in particular on the issuance of orders, save this, that your Honour will note at page 2 of the motion by the Prosecution that they offer someone up to give evidence about the efforts which have been made to get these people here. Orders of this kind are serious matters, which may involve compulsion upon those to whom it is directed, and it may be that your Honours would wish to take up the offer to give evidence that is made by my learned friend for the Prosecution. Can I move on from there and now I hope where, as one is bound to occasionally wear an amicus curia hat, all the proposed orders are in the first instance and if your Honours look at the proposed orders attached at the back of the motion, initially directed to a sovereign state, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The position as outlined by my learned friend as to the law is not perhaps quite as straightforward as he might have led your Honours to think. There is a problem that your Honours may wish to consider raised by the existence of the appeal lodged by the Republic of Croatia in relation to this very matter. That arises from a decision of 18th July 1997, with which two of your Honours will be well familiar, having sat on that decision and may be well taken to know the law in relation to that, and I refer here to Judge Jan and Judge Odio Benito. Also presiding in that case was Judge McDonald. There has subsequently been a decision of 29th July 1997, which was a decision of the Appeals Chamber, Judge President Cassese presiding, your Honour Judge Karibi-Whyte being part of that appeal Chamber and also Judges Li, Stephen and Vohrah. The effect of that decision -- if your Honour would just give me a moment, please -- looking at the final part of the order that was made by the Appeals Chamber, was to allow Croatia to appeal the subject matter of the decision of 18th July, rejecting Croatia's request to quash the subpoena that had been issued in that instance, but suspending the decision pending disposal of the present appeal by staying the execution of the subpoena. Can I also in this regard remind your Honours of what happened in another matter on 18th March 1997. There was a decision in Trial Chamber I, where Judges Jorda, Li and Riad, in the interests of uniformity of approach, referred a Defence motion, requesting the Chamber to issue a subpoena to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in order to compel the production of documents, to Judge McDonald, as she had before her at that stage related matters. The point is this: the consequences of the appeal which has been lodged by Croatia, it can go two ways: it can say that the original decision of 18th July was correct, that there is a lawful power within this Tribunal to issue subpoenas, or it may say, and one does not know what the decision will be until it is rendered, it may say that such orders are unlawful. Ponder for a moment what the possible consequences of the latter decision being made might be. If in the meantime orders issued to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which are subsequently found to have been unlawful, firstly the individuals who are ultimately the recipients of the order may find that their civil and human rights have been violated because of the execution of an unlawful order, and secondly, if during the course of execution of an unlawful order physical measures are taken to procure the attendance of witnesses, if the order is found to be unlawful, then the activities of laying hands upon the ultimate recipients, the individuals would amount to an assault. That is a serious matter. I mention this because although it is plain from the brief that was submitted by Bosnia-Herzegovina in the 18th July decision that they accept or concede that there is a lawful power, they may, of course, be wrong in the light of the appeal that is to be heard. It would be sensible in my submission to do two things here. Firstly, to enquire whether the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina does in fact have any views on whether there should be a stay in the light of the existing appeal; and secondly, your Honours may wish to consider whether the appropriate course, if you decide to issue an order, is to follow the procedure that has been taken in the Croatia case, in the interests of uniformity of approach, and suspend the execution of those orders. I raise those matters not because I particularly oppose the issue of subpoenas, because those may become important to the Defence just as to the Prosecution, but simply to alert your Honours to a potential pitfall which may cause all sorts of problems later on, and it is the uniformity of approach aspect that your Honours may feel is important to consider in this case. I hope those remarks are helpful. If there is anything I can assist any of your Honours on, I will be happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will be extremely brief. First of all, let me say that I think as a representative of Mr. Esad Landzo, or as a representative of any defendant in this case, that any standing we might have to discuss this issue is very limited, perhaps only to the question of whether or not the Prosecution has made a showing that the subpoena is likely to produce relevant evidence, so any remarks that I make this morning have to be, I think, in an amicus curiae kind of position. If I had an opportunity to argue the general issue before the appellate Chamber, which now has this matter under consideration, I would be heard to strongly urge the basic position taken by Mr. Niemann; that is that this Tribunal has, and should say that it has, the power to issue subpoenas. It will be virtually impossible for defendants appearing before this Tribunal, and brought before this Tribunal, to be able to have fair trials if they do not have the ability to subpoena witnesses in their Defence, especially in a situation where one of the governments in the former Yugoslavia is co-operative with one party to the litigation, but totally uncooperative with the other, so that one party to the litigation could have access to evidence that could not be countered by the other party because of no ability to subpoena. Those are the arguments that I would make if I were arguing to the appellate Chamber and it may very well be, as Mr. Greaves says, that we must await the decision of the appellate Chamber because, as I understand it, the issues before the appellate Chamber encompass everything down to the question of whether there is power to issue subpoenas at all, and that would be my submission. I thank you for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Moran?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, again let me put on my amicus hat and suggest this to the court. First, I think that the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina probably ought to be heard. As the Trial Chamber knows or may not know, at least in this case, the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina has been very co-operative with the Tribunal, to the extent that when the indictment against my client and Mr. Landzo was interned, they actually called them and told them to surrender themselves and they voluntarily -- the clients voluntarily surrendered themselves to the government who sent them here. With that said, the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina may very well take the position that we want to know from the appellate Chambers what our obligations are before we start doing anything. With that said, if I were appearing before the appellate Chamber, I would disagree with Mr. Niemann to this extent, on his argument; he looked at Articles 6, 8 and 9, saying this gives the Trial Chamber jurisdiction to issue this. I would say that in fact your powers may very well be broader than Mr. Niemann would suggest, by basing them on Articles 6, 8 and 9 of the Statute. Article 6 simply says you cannot try organisations like they did in Nuremberg, the Gestapo, you have to try people, and 8 and 9 talk about your authority to hear and decide cases. I think the authority to issue orders to government is somewhat broader than that. I would, for instance, happily defend the proposition that the Trial Chamber could issue a subpoena to the United States government ordering the United States to produce evidence, even though it is well outside the territory of the former Yugoslavia. But I think that the important thing at this point is firstly the uniformity we have talked about, I think we need to know what the appellate Chamber is going to say; and secondly I think someone ought to pick up the telephone and call the Bosnian Embassy here and offer them a chance to come in tomorrow or Friday morning, find out what the position of the Bosnian government is, to see whether they want to push to await a decision from the Appeals Chamber, to know exactly what their obligation is. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May I, your Honours, also address your Honours in connection with this issue. My learned colleague Mr. Niemann drew attention to the importance of the issues contained in the request for a subpoena, but at the same time he confirmed that there was no doubt that this Trial Chamber has the powers to issue such a subpoena. I think that my colleagues on the Defence have presented sufficient arguments to show why we need to think over very closely the consequences of such a premature decision, since in the Blaskic case the issue of the powers of this Tribunal to issue subpoenas is before the Appeals Chamber. In the arguments offered by the Prosecutor, it is stated that the position of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina is such that if the Trial Chamber issues the subpoena and the order it will follow through those orders. I personally am not familiar with the position of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, except as presented in the explanation, but as a person who has for more than 25 years been working in the judiciary, I could express my personal opinion, and that is that we should give preference to all the means and possibilities that would ensure the effectiveness of the procedure, but I personally would not go so far as to consider myself entitled to decide whether this Tribunal has those powers or not. I think that the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina has never felt that it is up to it to say what the competencies of the Tribunal are. Probably the government too is fully aware, like all of us here, that the position as to the authority of the Tribunal to issue a subpoena or not is up to the Tribunal itself to decide. Therefore, my country, like any other country, is awaiting the decision of the Appeals Chamber to see whether the Tribunal has that authority or not. As for the other questions that have been raised in connection with this matter, whether the Tribunal has established that it has the power to issue a subpoena, in that case, I feel that the party submitting such a proposal or request before the Tribunal has to make such a request a realistic one. Since Mr. Niemann and also my learned colleague Mr. Greaves have expressed certain views contained in national legislations, I should like to take the liberty, if that may be of any assistance in your determination, to familiarise you with the procedural code of Bosnia-Herzegovina according to which a national criminal court is entitled to subpoena a witness and in the case that the witness has no justified reason for not responding to the request for appearance, he may be called up under threat of penalty. Therefore we do not know whether in this case the witnesses had any justified reason for not appearing, and the national legislation of our country, which the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina is bound by, protects the citizens who for justified reasons are unable to respond to a court order. These competencies of the court are regulated by our procedural code, Articles 237 and Article 230. To another matter, we all know the situation in which Bosnia-Herzegovina finds itself. The dates indicated in the request of the Prosecution are such that even if such powers were established, it appears as if one wishes to issue an order that cannot be followed through, because it is that it is not possible to carry through an order issued today by tomorrow, so that I am not sure whether this request is well-founded and furthermore, whether it is realistic and implementable. Also, I agree with the proposal that a representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina should be invited to express the position of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina regarding this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: May I say something? The subpoena sought by the Prosecution -- I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Before any contribution, I attempted to see the argument of Niemann who divides the application into two parts, the part affecting the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the aspect affecting private individuals. A careful study of the case even on appeal clearly indicates that the second part is not in issue, so we have not had your comments on that aspect, whether his application is affected by the fact that the case is on appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I had just risen -- I am sorry, I did not mean to interrupt. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The subpoenas sought by the Prosecution affect five persons; four I believe are witnesses of fact, they have been asked to depose something which is within their personal knowledge. Can there be any objection to subpoena issued to an individual? You see the judgement in the Blaskic case, the issues are entirely different. There the state was asserting its sovereignty, saying that no subpoena can be issued to a sovereign state, but the question of issuing subpoena to four persons who are being asked to give evidence from their personal knowledge is an entirely different one. As regards the custodian who is being sought to produce documents and prove certain documents, maybe the question of issuing subpoena to a sovereign state is sub judice before the Appeals Chamber, but the argument was that you cannot issue subpoena to a sovereign state, it was not in dispute that a request can be made to a sovereign state, which will have, of course, the effect of an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I had risen, your Honour, to remind you of the terms of the appeal, it may be helpful to remind you of that. It is plain that it involves the rights of Croatia and sovereign states.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: And sovereign states, but they did not take the position that no request can be made to a sovereign state to comply with the order, and Article 29 would apply as much to a subpoena as to a request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually the objection appears essentially to be to the terminology used, to the word "subpoena" in its traditional common law sense. This is what they are objecting to, because devoid of its element of coercion, I suppose they might not be objecting. I agree that is still sub judice, there is nothing one can do about it until it is decided, but if one follows the provisions of Article 29 itself, I think perhaps there is still a way out of getting into conflict through the use of the word "subpoena".

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The proposed order is a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. I was just going to ask Mr. Niemann, instead of issuing a subpoena to the state with regard to four witnesses of fact, why cannot we issue a subpoena to those persons directly? They are being asked to appear as individuals, not as representatives or officials of the Bosnian government, but as individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am just turning to look at it, your Honour, because that was what I thought we had done. If there is anything that is confusing by what we have submitted in the motion, your Honour, then we would be anxious to correct that, but the way we have drafted the draft orders to the motion, it is separated. The first is an order to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and it is an order under 29(2). The second is in fact the subpoena which is or was intended to be directed to the individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The draft which is before me, the first one, is a subpoena to the Bosnian government to ensure that these four witnesses appear before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, what is requested is that the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina serve the subpoena, and then to ensure they appear on the dates mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is it a subpoena to the government then? It is not a subpoena to the officials?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, the subpoena, your Honours, is the second document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: To ensure that Asif and Jovan appear before the Tribunal. Why not issue a subpoena directly to them and request the Bosnian government to serve it upon them?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is what we have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But you are asking a subpoena to the government. Look at the heading of this, "Order to the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It may appear confusing, but there are two draft documents attached to your Honours' motion. The first motion is an order, the second one is a subpoena.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But then you are also saying "ensure". They can ensure service, but how can they ensure that they appear unless you give a subpoena to them?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But we are, your Honour. That is the second draft --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I said instead of directing the subpoena to the government, why not direct it to these four persons and request the Bosnian government to have it served upon them? It is a slightly different way of putting it, but the objection which is raised in the Blaskic case would disappear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is exactly what we have done, your Honour. There are two drafts. Does your Honour see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: They are alternate drafts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour should have two drafts attached to your motion. Perhaps your Honour's motion is deficient. You should have two drafts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I have two drafts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: One is to the individuals, which is the subpoena, and the other is the order which goes with the subpoena.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Why not substitute the word "order" with a "request", so the objection which is being raised in the Blaskic case and is under consideration before the Appeal Chamber, that will become irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Because of the plain words of Article 29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I know, but still the matter is there before the Appeal Chamber and I would not like to say something -- of course I was of the view, if we had the power, but then there is another view which has been canvassed in the court and our order has been suspended.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: These are draft orders, if your Honours are not happy with the wording of them, of course they can be changed. If your Honours prefer to proceed by way of request on first instance, obviously we have no objections to endeavouring to proceed that way. If your Honours feel more comfortable with that approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am quite comfortable as it is, but the question of the matter is before the Appeal Chamber. I am quite comfortable with all the drafts, speaking personally, because I am party to the decision. I am quite comfortable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps if I could address a couple of matters, your Honours? I agree with your Honour that the Blaskic appeal which is presently under consideration is related to the issue of subpoena against the state, which is a controversial question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: And may even extend to orders to sovereign states.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I understand what your Honour says, and for that reason, changing the word to "request" from "order" would be an appropriate move. The question of bringing the government here, there is two responses I have to that. One is that we can say that from our position there is nothing to suggest -- nothing that has been suggested to us which would indicate that they are not willing to comply with the provisions of Article 29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: May I tell you something? While the matter is being argued, two counsel appeared on behalf of Bosnia-Herzegovina. One is Madam Vidovic, then there was a Croat lady also. The Croat lady took the position we do not have the power, but Madam Vidovic, she said yes, we have the power. I wonder if you were there when the arguments were being heard?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My response to that, your Honour, is that the part of the government to which these people are connected, we believe, may be covered by the ambit of jurisdiction of Madam Vidovic. I cannot put it any other way, but in terms of them appearing and if one is precious of the rights of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina to be heard on this matter, I would say that the rules do not necessarily envisage that they need to be called in first instance, because that would have to be done by way of amicus. They have no rights as a party. But the rules do envisage protection of their rights by Rule 108bis, which specifically gives them a right of review in the event that your Honours were to make an interlocutory order of this nature, and it is something that can be brought on quickly, can be brought on within 15 days, so if one is concerned about the rights of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there is provision in the rules to cater for that, and that can be done quickly. It is not a question of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina not knowing anything about this, I can say that they are well aware of what we are doing and certainly have the documentation before them, so it is not as though we are doing this without them knowing what is happening. In terms of people not complying for good reason, of course that is what a subpoena is about. It is implicit in any subpoena that if a person has a good reason for non-compliance, then they are not met with a sanction for failure to attend, and although the rules of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the law of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as referred to by Madam Residovic, may be worded perhaps differently, the end result is the same. Obviously if someone cannot attend and if there is good reason why those people are refusing to come, that is a matter that your Honours will no doubt take into account when dealing with that question, but it is not a basis upon which an order is not sought in first instance. One seeks the order, one seeks the subpoena and then if people cannot comply with it, it is for them to come forward and give good reason. They can appoint counsel or do whatever is necessary so that the Chamber can be informed. Obviously if they present good reason for their refusal to attend, that is a matter that the Chamber can have full regard to. Finally, I just conclude by saying that I do not believe that the issue before the Appeals Chamber relates to an individual -- subpoena against an individual and I do not consider therefore that there is any real danger of people being subpoenaed on an order that may subsequently be found to be invalid, but even if it were so, there is a presumption of validity of your Honours' orders. Your Honours are entitled to proceed at the moment on the basis of the law, there is nothing in the law to suggest your Honours cannot do this, and in my submission, it is clear that your Honours can do it, there is a presumption of validity. Even if the Appeal Chamber did come to a conclusion that subpoena was not within the power of the Tribunal, that would have no impact legally upon the orders that your Honours would issue which would be deemed to be valid and legal and only those orders appealed against in any event could be held to be illegal, but even so, they would be presumed valid until such time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: There are four matters I want to raise with your Honours. I suspect my learned friend has not read his own draft. The heading of the draft to Bosnia-Herzegovina says "order" and on the second page, it says "hereby directs" and it contains as its final paragraph this: "Further directs in the event of non-compliance with this order by the government that a representative of the government appear before the Trial Chamber on a named date to show why this order has not been complied with." It does not sound like a polite request to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It can be redrafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes, but I think my learned friend did not quite read that last paragraph when he used the word "request".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do resent the insinuation that I have not read the orders. It is extraordinary arrogance to say that. This arose as a discussion between myself and His Honour Judge Jan as to whether or not perhaps the word "order" should be changed to "request". For counsel then to have the temerity to get up and suggest I have not read it is frankly quite unnecessary and insulting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If he feels insulted I apologise. However, let us just make it absolutely plain what he is asking for. That is what he is asking for, to direct, not request. The second matter is this, these orders may well become de rigeur in due course, particularly in view of the determination of the appeal. However, at the present time it may well be at the very least a sensible courtesy to enquire of the Bosnian government if they wish to be heard on this matter, so as we know exactly what the position is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But Mr. Greaves, issuance of a request has not been in controversy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Indeed no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: So why the representative of the Bosnian government at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I am merely suggesting that as a sensible courtesy, if nothing else, they may wish to be heard in some way. They may say "we do not wish to be heard, it is not a problem", but until the issue has been determined on appeal, it may be no more than that, I am merely suggesting it. If your Honours think it is a bad idea, then I do not pursue it. The terms of the appeal your Honours will be familiar with, but there is one matter that arises out of it. In the application for video-link, the Prosecution asserted that two of the witnesses who are the subject of this subpoena request are in fact serving officers of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army. One of the issues that has been raised is the issuance of orders to sovereign states and their officials acting in an official capacity. That is a matter that I raise that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: They are going to depose something which is within their personal knowledge, nothing to do with their official work, official responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I can see an argument for saying that I might not concede that, your Honour. If they are deposing to matters carried out during the terms of their official capacity, then it may well be arguable that they are acting in their official capacity, but I do not particularly want to get involved in a long semantic argument, but I merely alert your Honours to that as a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Greaves. I think there is a necessary judicial caution at a time when the matter is on appeal to find a way to deal with it, so we will rise for a few minutes and discuss how to deal with the intricate matter. It is a little problem. We will come back at 12.00 and then we will indicate our decision. (11.15 am) (A short break) (12.00 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has decided on making a very short ruling. We have decided to grant the application. Now let me read the ruling. The Trial Chamber has heard the Prosecution in this application for a subpoena, firstly against the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its custodian of records. The subpoena also seeks another against Asif Paselic, Esad Ramic, Jovan Divjak, Kemal Dzajic and Fadil Zebic to attend before the Trial Chamber to testify in respect of matters within their personal knowledge. Counsel to the Defence, Mr. Greaves, John Ackerman, Tom Moran and Ms. Residovic appeared as amici curiae and made very valuable contributions, for which the Trial Chamber is very appreciative and grateful. The Prosecution pointed out that it relied on the jurisdiction of the Tribunal in Articles 6, 8 and 9 of the Statute and the enabling provisions of Article 29(2). It was admitted that the Trial Chamber has the statutory provision to make the order by virtue of Article 29(2) and Rule 54 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Trial Chamber is entirely in agreement with this, but we fear there are certain definitional inaccuracies which we would point out later. The amici curiae pointed out that the question of issuing a subpoena against it is pending in the Appeals Chamber and the Trial Chamber should be wary in dealing with the question. They all implored caution. We entirely agree, and the Trial Chamber is aware of the fact that the issue of the subpoena against sovereign states is sub judice. The Trial Chamber appreciates that it cannot, as the law stands, grant the application without being conscious of the specific provisions of Article 29, but we agree it had jurisdiction under Rule 4 to make the application. We agree also that under Rule 54, the Trial Chamber can grant the issue of subpoena against private individuals. Further, Article 29 vests in the Trial Chamber the power to make an order in respect of requests to sovereign states. On account of these statutory powers, the Trial Chamber, having considered the submissions of the Prosecutor, have decided to grant the application within the terms of Article 29(2). We therefore grant the request to Bosnia-Herzegovina -- the requests, and not the application of the subpoena to Bosnia-Herzegovina and to the custodian of records of its government. The application for subpoena against the named persons to testify before the Trial Chamber is also hereby granted. This is our ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If it please your Honours. Your Honours, I just would indicate at this stage that if now as a consequence of your Honours' orders any of the witnesses raise with us any genuine difficulties in complying with the attendance dates of the subpoenas, we will raise these before you and if it is appropriate seek a variation of the actual dates, but I just should say we will do that if it occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: At the time we heard the argument there was no issue of change of dates, so we left the dates as they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: So we can now continue with the proceedings. I wish to express our gratitude to all the amici curiae again. It was quite helpful. Not that we are not conscious or aware of the fact that there are a few fresh lights which were thrown on the problems true of the problems which might arise. The Tribunal believes we should try to work outside the field so that we can get it without any conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may take up a brief housekeeping matter while we are waiting for the witness to appear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, yesterday, towards the end of the day, with respect to Witness J, I asked that the prior statements be admitted into evidence as they relate to impeachment. I believe your Honours granted that. The Registrar has told me that she wishes in open court to give them the numbers, so, just as a housekeeping matter, I would just like the Registrar to state the numbers of those two exhibits. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibits are 183 and 184.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can you bring the witness in now? (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly swear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I should like to remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: His microphone is probably not working.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I proceed, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed. WITNESS R (continued)

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. R. Yesterday before the break talking about the conditions of life inside hangar number 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, just one second, your Honour, I am sorry to interrupt, but looking at the transcript we are seeing “continuation of Witness J", and I just wanted to make sure that the record is clear that this is Mr. R so that at some point in the future --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Again I apologise for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Moran. We were talking yesterday about the conditions of life in hangar 6 and you were talking about drinking water supplies. Could you please tell us about food supplies in the time when you were in hangar 6, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether I said everything regarding water supplies, I said that it was industrial water, but if I may add a few sentences in connection with the water and the bathing, after the second attack on Bradina on 12th July when it was burned down, July 1992, no water could be kept in the hangar --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object. This witness has on frequent occasions paid no attention to the question and said "I am going to answer something else first". In this case the question was about the food supplies and he just volunteered that there were things he wanted to say about the water without any question being asked. It seems to me that, at a very minimum, the witness should be asked to respond to the question asked rather than going off on his own and making speeches. That would be my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think the Prosecutor should remind him to answer the question he asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. R, I ask you to be responsive to my question. We might go back to that with any other question, but please give us your account about food supplies now inside hangar 6, if you do not mind, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well, as you wish. At first, when we were imprisoned, for the first two days we got no food. This was in tunnel number 9. However, as your question was very precise, and it referred to number 6, let me talk about number 6. Food consisted mostly of stale bread, made of stale flour and mouldy flour, and it had a very unpleasant taste. The quantity was such that a loaf was divided up among 14 or 15 or even more parts, so these were very thin slices of bread, with which most frequently we got nothing. Occasionally, we would get some cold soup, which would be several days old, but the problem was how to eat the soup in hangar number 6 in which there were between 250 and 270 prisoners; there were only five spoons. There were no plates or other containers, but the soup was poured into a lid.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Excuse me for a moment. (Pause). You may go ahead, Mr. R. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soup was poured into a lid and there were only five spoons, so that the people who brought the soup would pour some into a lid and five prisoners would use the five spoons and grab as much as they could from that lid, then leave the spoons and then the next five would come and eat in the same way. It is interesting to note where we ate, where the food was distributed. It was right next to the door of the hangar, I do not know if it is necessary for me to show you where on the drawing, this was right next to the door, and during the night, at that same place, the prisoners relieved themselves during the night, because they were not allowed to go out. So that that same spot would be just washed away with a hose in the morning or some water would be sprinkled on it and that was the place where we met. Occasionally, there would be an ammunition box or a rifle box on which that lid would be placed, and the spoons would sometimes fall on the ground, but they could never be washed, so that 250 to 270 prisoners, depending on the number at the time, would eat with five spoons, which were never washed in between. That is as far as the food supply is concerned and the hygiene and also the water in a sense, and I apologise for going back to that all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. R, was there any time when you remained without food or without drinking water during the entire day during your stay in hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I remember for sure 28th June, because that is a kind of Serbian national holiday and the gentlemen who were guarding us knew better when those holidays were than we ourselves, because we had no calendars or anything else, so for sure on June 28th we got nothing, no food nor water. The same occurred on 12th July when, according to the old orthodox calendar, it is Saint Peter's day and when Bradina was burned down for a second time so that certainly that date was not chosen by chance, so those two days we were left totally without food or water.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you now tell us about sleeping facilities inside hangar 6? How did you sleep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said last time that we were all given positions where we had to sit and from which we were not allowed to move. We were also supposed to sleep on those same positions, crouching down with our knees up, without the right to utter a word, so what we would do, we would just sort of stretch out on the concrete, on the same position at which we sat. Let me also mention in connection with sleeping that after 12th July Mr. Delic issued special orders that no one should sleep for three days, and during the night the guards would come very frequently. Not only were we not allowed to sleep, but we were not allowed to lie down, we had to sit with our knees up and the guards would check repeatedly to make sure that the prisoners would not change positions, and the position of basluci, the name given to us frequently by Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you now tell us something about the toilet facilities in general while you were staying in hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning, for urination purposes five people could go out together and use a canal which was situated directly behind number 6. As for other toilet needs, there was a pit dug out just behind hangar number 6, a pit was dug out with a plank on it and this was used as a toilet or whatever you like to call it. Later on, as time went by, and as the conditions became worse, Mr. Delic introduced his own methods so that later it was not allowed for five people to go out at a time, but five lines corresponding to the five rows in the hangar, people would have to stand up to form a line, one behind the other, to run out, then again to form a line, a straight line to urinate and then to run back again in a straight line and to sit back in his position, and he would measure the time, he would time this, and this took, I think, less than a minute, because when the International Red Cross came, and when this gentleman, I think his name was Michel, timed this he said it was 40 seconds and he just lifted his hands in wonder. That was an original invention of Mr. Delic's. As for going to the toilet, at first we were allowed to go when we needed to, but later on there was a system of numbers introduced and during the day only 15 people could go out who were given numbers, the others had to stay inside, so that during the night when people had bowel movement they had to do it inside right next to the door. At first there was -- something, I do not know how to call it, like a bucket, it was plastic, but it would always fill to capacity, it was a small bucket and I said there were 250 to 270 prisoners, with the number varying. It was always overspilling, so that it covered the whole area around the door where we were served the soup the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. R. Let us go to another topic now. Were you ever interrogated by military investigators while you were in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, once.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say approximately when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact date, but the interrogation came -- I was among the last to be interrogated because the people believed what they were told, that as soon as they were heard they would be released, so people were rushing to get there first, so that I was among the last to be interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say, where in the camp were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was interrogated at the command building, not inside but outside. There was a table on the model between that building and building number D, as it is marked here. We were called by the guards, we had to line up and go towards the command building, then we were lined up against the wall, I personally had to stand against the wall of building number C with my hands raised up high for at least, I assume, four hours, and the heat of Herzegovina that can sweep Celebici and with my bald head, without being allowed to put your hands down or to ask for water -- when my turn came for the interrogation, the interrogator, I think his name was Subasic, he brought me to the table after spending so long standing and when he started asking me questions, and actually I could hardly speak, I had no voice, because it had dried up, because of dehydration, and this exposure to the summer sun without water, then he called one of the guards to bring a glass of water, and that is when the interrogation started. Mr. Subasic said, "we know everything, absolutely everything and we need no new information, but to satisfy the procedure, do not even try to tell a lie".

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was Mr. Subasic the only person who interrogated you? I mean, were there any other people together with him during this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With me, or rather at the table, there was Mr. Subasic, but the guards were around, but they did not ask any questions, they were just armed and they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was Mr. Subasic in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How were you treated during the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the interrogation itself, no kind of violence was resorted to, except for this previous period of dehydration before I sat at the table. I can say that Mr. Subasic was relatively correct during the interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: During the interrogation, were you accused of anything specific?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was that a long interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the interrogation was very short, I do not think it was ever completed actually. Nor did Mr. Subasic show me what he wrote, nor did I sign anything. I think that probably in his opinion it had not been completed. Why it was not resumed later, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What did he ask you? Do you remember any specific question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the standard questions at first, my name, occupation, age, and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did he ask you about your weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. He asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What did you answer about your weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I had this old or obsolete M48 rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, you said you were about -- among the last ones to be interrogated. As far as you know, was any prisoner interrogated at the very beginning, during the time you still were in tunnel 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the interrogation started already at that time for some people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you mention the name of any of the prisoners who were interrogated at that early time when you still were in tunnel 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this was on the second or third day. Among the first was Dragan Kuljanin, and I do not remember any other names.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Who was this Dragan Kuljanin? How old was he and what did he do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was an electrician, he worked in Konjic, in the Igman factory, and I think he was born somewhere in 1960 or 1962, I do not know exactly. I know that he was beaten up very badly, he had a leg injury and he limped when he went for the interrogation. I know he had great problems with the joint of his leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did this Dragan Kuljanin tell you anything about his interrogation right after coming back to the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he said that the investigator was to have been the judge, Goran Lokas, and that he had refused, saying, "I will not interrogate such people who have been massacred in this way".

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question calls for hearsay, not just what Dragan Kuljanin said but what Dragan Kuljanin said somebody else said, so it is twice removed hearsay at this point, with no foundation of reliability whatsoever, not even any foundation that Dragan Kuljanin actually heard something from Goran Lokas, but it is hearsay that is going through at least two steps and perhaps beyond that and I think for that reason it is inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: If I may respond, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: My submission is that Dragan Kuljanin referred something immediately after his interrogation and he referred what the person who interrogated him and this I think corresponds to the general principles for reliability of hearsay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Did he say that immediately after that gentleman said he was not prepared to sit on the investigation board? You are talking about someone else. He might have heard it six months ago from someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. (Pause). Mr. R, when did Dragan Kuljanin tell you all this? Was that right after his interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: These remarks must have been made much earlier before this gentleman was detained himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We are talking about the first week of detention of Witness R.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Listen, let us go back and ask him the question. Let him answer again and waste no more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. The question was: did Dragan Kuljanin tell you who interrogated him and anything about his interrogation right after coming back to the tunnel, right after this interrogation had taken place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said at that time that the chief judge during this investigation -- in this interrogation was going to be Goran Lokas, but that he refused, saying that he did not want to interrogate massacred people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now there is not even any indication that he talked to Goran Lokas, that he was not even there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What he was saying is what the gentleman told him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But we have no identification of who it was that told him about Goran Lokas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is a different matter. He is telling you what he was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He is telling us, your Honour, what he was told by Dragan Kuljanin, that someone else had apparently told Dragan Kuljanin about what someone else had said. That is the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What he was told at the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It has not even been established who it was that was interviewing Dragan Kuljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is a different matter. He went for an interview and this was what he was told there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question must be, for hearsay purposes, your Honour, who it was that made this statement to Dragan Kuljanin that Dragan Kuljanin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is not relevant, that does not concern him. What concerns him is what he was told. If in deliberating it we find that what was being told is too remote or has nothing to do with what we are doing here, we might -- so let him say what he was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me then only request that the Prosecutor establish who it was that said whatever was said to Dragan Kuljanin. I think that is now in serious question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are going backwards, behind Dragan, that is a different matter. Kuljanin was merely speaking to this witness and this witness is merely interested to tell us what he was told by Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you personally know who Goran Lokas was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew because Goran Lokas was a judge. Personally I was never in touch with him, I never contacted him, I just know that he was a lawyer and a judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go to another issue, Mr. R. Did you personally suffer any physical maltreatment; I mean any other physical maltreatment during your stay in Celebici besides the beating on the very first day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but not as much as some other people did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you receive personally, not meaning group beatings, personally particular mistreatment and can you tell us how many times and give us an account of these occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally was beaten twice, that is up until the visit of the International Red Cross, on which occasion we were all beaten up, so let me go back to those two occasions. The first time it was Mr. Zenga that took me out and he slapped me hard, but that was not a bad beating. At that time there was a guard in front of the hangar, Rustem Murici who was an Albanian and who I knew for about ten years before the war started and who said to Mr. Zenga, "do not beat up this person for no reason, for no good reasons", things like that, approximately like that. That is what he said. Then Zenga turned around to him and Zenga said, "who did I ever beat up and was not ordered to do so?" So that was the end of that. In comparison to other kinds of beating, this slap was nothing, but in a sense it was beating, it was mistreatment. The second time, the second beating was in the hangar itself, Mr. Zenga used to walk around and to force the prisoners to do push-ups and as people were starved and they were deprived of water and he would order them to do 10, 15 push-ups, they would be able to do one or two and then they would fall down into the dust, on their nose or on their stomachs. Then Mr. Zenga would stand them up by kicking them with his boot, and there I got two hard kicks. The last beating that I received was the third day after the visit of the International Red Cross, which was on 13th, 14th August. So that was on 13th August, the second day, when the visit was finished and the representatives asked for statements on the conditions, of the number of dead and their names. When they left, Mr. Delic came in with the entire guard, there were about 15 of them, and there was another guard there who was not on duty at that time who was a former policeman in the old Federal Police, and his nickname was Focak. Then we were ordered to sit up in our usual position and the position was to put your hands up behind your head and these 15 -- with Mr. Delic and Mr. Focak there were 17 of them altogether -- so all guards would pass by the prisoners and would kick them in the kidney area or lower back or around the spine, would kick them with their boots. So they were passing and every prisoner would get these kicks from 15 guards and Delic was saying, "I will give you your Red Cross".

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Going back to the beating you personally received from Mr. Zenga, doing the push-ups, did Mr. Zenga say anything while doing this to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I could not remember that now. I could not recall specific words or sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Can you say the complete name of this guard named Zenga?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His last name is Landzo, everybody called him Zenga, his first name could be Omer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How did you get to know his name and his nickname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learned from other prisoners. I did not know this man, Mr. Zenga, before arriving at number 6, but after these beatings, after being taken out, I asked, "who is this person who is taking persons out?", and they said, "this is Zenga and he is the leader of the people who beat prisoners".

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. R, did you personally eyewitness any mistreatment of any other prisoners while you were in hangar 6? Could you please tell us if you eyewitnessed incidents like that one by one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know where to start from, because there was no order to it in all these beatings. I do not know where to start, with beatings, with deaths.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Let us start with the incidents which did not cause the death of anybody.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those incidents were a daily occurrence, so to speak. When the night came, that is right after dusk, that would be about 10.00 or 11.00 in the mid summer, the door would open and at the entrance, without coming in, Zenga would call out persons who needed to come out. He would call them by their first and last name. He could conclude that it was Zenga by his voice, by his timbre, because it was a very characteristic voice. It was almost a whining voice and it is almost to being feminine sounding. Also it was characteristic the way he called people out, he would say, "Vukasin, come out", or Hristo Vukalo for instance, he would just say "Vukalo".

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Let us please give an account one by one of these, specifically about these incidents, with details you could eyewitness, personally observe, anyway personally.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could personally speak to two deaths, Milorad Kuljevic and Bosko Mrkajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I am sorry, Mr. R, just for a reason of order, let us talk about deaths later on and let us talk about incidents which did not end with the death of anybody first, if you do not mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would always start with calling out the person and this person would come out and then the beatings would usually be carried out in front of number 6 on this concrete --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I am sorry, Mr. R, could you please wait for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we will have a break here for lunch while you organise your examination, be able to know exactly what issues to talk about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. (1.00 pm) (Adjourned until 2.30 pm) 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25 (2.30 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly invite the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask something while we are waiting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In my mind at least, it continues to be a problem that when we argue legal matters that the witness tends to get involved in those arguments; not just this witness, I am referring to what is a continuing problem. I know it concerns all of us and I believe it concerns the Office of the Prosecutor, my esteemed colleague Mr. Niemann supported a previous objection I made in that regard and I have a suggestion. It may make sense, if it is not too disruptive, when clearly there is going to be extended legal argument, for the witness to be asked to remove his headphones. If he cannot hear what is going on, he cannot make contributions to it. The other thing that would accomplish is it would keep the witness from being educated by either party as to what we might expect that witness to say when finally asked the question. I do not know if that is workable, but it may be a solution. I just wanted to pass it along to the Trial Chamber for your consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I also make two brief comments?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: (redacted) As I do not speak English I have not compared the translation, but I have been told that there is a word which changes the meaning from the negative to the positive, so I would ask the court translators to compare the two versions after which we can submit the best translation to the Registry. A second point I should like to make is a question addressed to Mr. Niemann; in view of your ruling this morning, Esad Ramic has been summoned as a witness. I have asked several times whether the Prosecutor has spoken to this witness, and if they have any statement of his could it be given to the Defence, so that we might prepare ourselves for the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You have named a protected witness just now. We will have to redact the name from the record. You were referring to the statement made yesterday, he is a protected witness and we refer to him as Mr. J, so for the name, you can put the word Mr. J in the redacted record. Is that your objection, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour, I was going to rise in relation to the other matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise and thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think we may be asking for redaction, I will have that organised. Your Honours, I just rise in relation two matters. Firstly in connection with the witness Ramic who has been subpoenaed. The answer is no, we do not have a statement, but we will try to assist the Defence by providing them with what we anticipate he will attest to, and there may be documents that we may refer to and we also refer their attention to that. In relation to the matter raised by Mr. Ackerman, we do support Mr. Ackerman in that, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, it is one of some difficulty, especially when it involves witnesses who become agitated, I do not know what for, and they want to get into the argument themselves.
