I prefer finding a solution to it. We will think about a solution which can remove them during such arguments; it is not even merely removing the headphones but completely removing them, but usually everyone is not too sure how extensive the argument will be, so that is another problem, but I think we will try as much as possible to make witnesses appreciate that. It is not for their benefit that the arguments are going on, it is for other purposes, so we will do our best.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if it is of any assistance to you, it is the practice we applied in the Tadic case, and it seemed to work reasonably well. It does save the inconvenience of having the witness coming and going all the time, especially when they are protected witnesses, and it is necessary to put the blinds up and down and that sort of thing. It did work reasonably successfully, if that is of any assistance to your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually some of our problems -- we thought here that the witness should come in before we came in but we are having difficulties in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. Now that your Honour has raised that, I was going to raise it later this afternoon, and ask whether or not that could be a practice, having regard to what I have seen in the memorandum that has been sent by the Registrar. It is a matter of great concern to us and I was going to ask the Chamber if you would indulge us by permitting the witnesses to come in after your Honours are sitting, so as to prevent that from happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we will (inaudible).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us have the witness. (Pause). (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly remind the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I am reminding you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I proceed, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you. So, Mr. R, could you please describe in detail and specifically the incidents that you personally observed and can remember one by one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps I should begin with the pouring of petrol --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Turone, maybe it would be more convenient if you can ask him if a particular person was in hangar number 6 at the relevant time and so what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: If your Honour would prefer me to ask every single prisoner --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Relating to a particular person, ask him if he was there in the hangar. This would be cut short. I think this was what Mr. Niemann was doing, "was such and such a person there and what happened?".

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I will proceed like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I do not think the Defence has any objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Not at all, your Honour, I think that is the preferred practice, to do a question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So Mr. R, do you know a person by the name of Vukasin Mrkajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was he also a prisoner inside hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was also a prisoner. May I thank the court for this suggestion because it facilitates my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. R. So, did you observe any incident concerning Mr. Vukasin Mrkajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as Vukasin Mrkajic is concerned, he was beaten almost daily by any one of the guards or by the deputy commander Delic, whenever he would come in. He was one of the targets and he was regularly beaten; but let me focus on one particular detail of the torture to which Vukasin Mrkajic was exposed. Some slow-burning fuse was wound around his body, Mr. Zenga came to the door and called Vukasin out, and I witnessed his going out the door, and a few minutes later, Vukasin came back and he had this fuse wrapped around his waist. One end was inside his trousers and Zenga was following him and the fuse was burning and he was jumping up and down, because it was causing burns, so when he came in, he was jumping about, trying to prevent the contact between the fuse and his body . Zenga followed him and ordered him to sit down in his place, which was predetermined for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you have any chance to personally see the blisters caused by the fuse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the blisters were all over the body. These were blisters filled with liquid which later burst, so that they turned into open wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did Zenga say anything during this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this moment, I cannot recall any particular words that he spoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did Vukasin Mrkajic receive any medical care after this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Vukasin Mrkajic was never given any kind of medical care or treatment and when he addressed Mr. Delic, if he had the occasion to do that, the answer he was given would be, "you have to die anyway so sit down".

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you know a person, I think you mentioned him, named Hristo Vukalo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know Hristo Vukalo, he was also a prisoner with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you observe any incident concerning this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Hristo Vukalo was treated in the same way with this fuse being wrapped around his waist, in the identical manner as with Mrkajic. He was called out outside, Zenga took him out and then he came back with the burning fuse round his waist, and he had to sit down, so that the procedure was virtually identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: About Hristo Vukalo, could you observe -- do you remember having personally observed any burns caused by the fuse on him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did see the burns, and in addition to that, there were haematoma on the body of Hristo Vukalo because he was several times before that and after that beaten severely, his whole body, his back was totally black and blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you remember Zenga having said anything during this incident, the fuse incident concerning Hristo Vukalo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember anything specific, I just know that he called him out in his specific tone of voice, calling out, "Vukalo", and then that he accompanied him back, so I cannot recall any particular words or phrases that he used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Did Hristo Vukalo receive any medical care after that incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you know a man by the name Mirko Babic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was he also prisoner in hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you observe or eyewitness in whole or in part any incident concerning Mirko Babic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Regarding Mirko Babic, he was also taken out or called out by Zenga and he came back with trousers which were still smoking. They were burning and the edges were still smoking. I remember that when we asked later on during the night, we asked him what had happened to him, he said that Zenga had poured some petrol or some other inflammable liquid on his lower legs and that he had set fire to it, and that is how the burns had occurred. There were blisters with lymph inside and these burst and one could almost see the bone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You mean you could personally see the blisters on the leg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: From which distance could you see this injury, on which occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The distance between my place and his was about five or six people in between, but sitting very close to one another, so those injuries could be seen when we would run out to go to the toilet or to urinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you describe this blister as much as you can in detail? Was that on one leg or both legs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, it was on one leg, but the distance between me and Mr. Babic was, as I said, five or six people between us. But there were other instances of such burnings, the consequences of which I could see very close up. I could mention the case of Dusko Bendzo and Nedeljko Draganic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We will go to that too in due course, but can you say approximately, very approximately when did Mirko Babic receive this injury on the leg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you thinking of the date, the period of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: At least the month.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was probably in August.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did Mirko Babic receive any medical care after this burn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, though Mirko Babic did ask Mr. Delic to give him any kind of medical assistance, but Delic's response was, "where is your son now to help you?", though Delic knew well that Mirko Babic was not married and that he had no children. He would add, "you have to die anyway". That was a favourite phrase that Mr. Delic used in his communication with the prisoners; "sit down, you have to die anyway, whether you are given medical assistance or not".

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did Mirko Babic receive any other mistreatment besides this burn on the leg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was exposed to daily beatings, and a special type of mistreatment were these constant threats and questions, "where is your son?", because we all knew that he was born somewhere in the 30s, 33, 35, we knew that he was a forest warden and that he was never married, so this was done intentionally to hurt his feelings, because he was not married.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What about the beatings you were talking about? Did you personally see, by whom was he beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was beaten in person by Delic and by Zenga. During the night he was called out by Zenga, now who was with him I cannot claim, because it was night-time, so I could not see, but when it happened in the hangar, it was Hazim Delic and Zenga who personally beat him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did these beatings occur before or after the burn on the leg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there were beatings before and after.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right, Mr. R, so you were saying something about Dusko Bendzo. Did you then observe an incident concerning him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as Dusko Bendzo, he was also taken out many times and beaten, but let me answer your question regarding burns. He was also called out in front of number 6 by Mr. Zenga, and we heard his cries or moans, and then Bendzo returned, again accompanied by Zenga, to his place. Both his lower legs were terribly burnt. He had on him a red sweat suit which was burnt up to the knees. It was totally burnt as far as the knees, and on the bones of his lower legs, one could see very large blisters which were soon filled with lymph, so these were large blisters which burst shortly afterwards, so that on both legs, one could see the bone right through, the burnt meat and the bone. I must add that Dusko Bendzo was not in the first row next to me, but the next row, quite opposite me, so that I could see those injuries every day. I could see them much better than in the case of Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you remember Zenga saying anything during this incident or on the occasion of this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not recall exactly now. I cannot remember the details now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did Dusko Bendzo receive any medical care after this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because Dusko Bendzo was also on Delic's list of those who had to die, so that when he too asked for any medical assistance, he got the same answer, "sit down, you have to die anyway".

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You were talking about Nedeljko Draganic also. Did you observe any incident concerning Nedeljko Draganic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nedeljko too was taken out several times and beaten during the night, but as for the same system of burning legs, I remember also an occasion when Mr. Zenga called him out, and that he was brought back escorted by him. He was sitting right in the row directly opposite me, facing me, so that I could observe that wound or the burn from a distance of maybe two metres every day. His trousers were also burnt through, and as far as I can remember that was only on his right leg, it was not on his left leg but on the right leg, in the case of Mr. Draganic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you describe this injury on the leg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was not the whole length of the shin, as in the case of Mr. Bendzo, whose wound was really terrible. This was more like a round wound affecting the muscle and the tissue, but in time, probably because of the dirt in the environment and because of the bacteria, the wound festered and it spread and there may even have been a danger of total infection of the leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you remember Zenga having said anything during this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not remember. I only know that in connection with Draganic himself, Mr. Delic told Zenga to take him away and to carve in the Chetnik sign on his forehead, but for some reason, he either forgot -- he failed to do it anyway, because the comment was, "you had this sign on your cap at a party once", and as Nedeljko said it was not true, Delic told Zenga, "take it away and carve it in so that he does not forget", but probably preoccupied with the beating of other prisoners, he probably forgot to carry out those orders. I do not know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did Nedeljko Draganic receive any medical care after the burn on the leg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that Nedeljko was taken to the infirmary and that for a time, he had some kind of a bandage on the wound. Whether there was any other medication used, antibiotics or anything like that I do not know, but I think for a time he did wear a bandage, but not for long.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. R, do you know a man by the name of (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was he also prisoner in hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you personally observe any incident concerning this man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) was also taken out several times during the night and beaten, but I remember an incident when Zenga took him out, or rather he called him out from the door, and when he came back, he had very large burns on both palms of his hands, and they swelled up very soon into large blisters, like balls. These blisters covered his palms entirely, and they were full of liquid too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did (redacted) tell you how he got these blisters on his hands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he said that Zenga had put a heated knife or a bayonet on to his palms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did (redacted) receive any medical care after this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. R, do you know a man by the (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was also a prisoner in hangar number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you personally observe any incident concerning (redacted) (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the very same story, so to say. He was also brought out, called out by Zenga, he went out and when he came back he had very heavy burns, which also then were filled with lymph and then broke, so the skin disappeared and the flesh was exposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did (redacted) tell you anything about how he received these blisters, these injuries on the hands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he said that Zenga also put this knife over a fire and then that the knife that was thus heated was then placed on the palms of his hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you remember Zenga having said anything, (redacted) (redacted) out of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not beside that. I do not know if he said anything else, I just do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Did (redacted) receive any medical care after this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you know a man by the name Mirko Djordjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was also a prisoner in hangar number 6 in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you observe personally any incident concerning Mirko Djordjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the same case as with the others, all the people I have already mentioned, it was a similar incident that occurred outside, I did not see it personally, I did not see the knife being placed there, but it was the same scenario, he was called out by Zenga and he used to call Mirko "Vojvoda's brother" because he was the brother of Rajko Djordjic who was for some reason proclaimed by them to be a Vojvoda, so he would say "come on, Vojvoda's brother, come out". When he came back he had burns on his face and his tongue and he told us that Zenga put a heated knife against his tongue under threat that if he did not stick his tongue out that he would cut it off. Then he also had visible burns on his face, on his cheeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did Mirko Djordjic receive any medical care after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Again, did you personally eyewitness any mistreatment of a sexual nature committed against any prisoners inside hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was an incident, I do not know how to call it, an act of violence committed against the brothers Dordic. It is not just a common incident. Vaso and Veseljko Djordjic were brought in from the village of Zukici several days after we were already in hangar number 6. Veseljko is the youngest of the two and so Vaso was older and the younger brother had his arm broken. I remember him, he wore a red -- he was wearing a red sweat suit, and the top was very short, and he had a splint on the forearm and it was tied with two bandages. I witnessed that whole incident, that beating, because Zenga did this right in the hangar in the presence of all the prisoners. Zenga was beating Veseljko, that is the younger brother who had this broken arm, and he was asking him whether he had a rifle, he said he did not, then Zenga continued beating him, until Veseljko said, "yes, I did have a rifle". "Were you meeting with Chetniks in Bradina?", he said he did not, and then the beating continued until Veseljko said that he did. Then the question was, "did you take food to the Chetniks" and Veseljko said yes, so all following questions were answered by "yes" so that he would prevent further torture. "Did you have machine-gun?", yes. "Did you have this, did you have an aeroplane", yes, so Zenga himself started laughing in the end, after having asked him all these questions of what he had. Then he ordered him to unbutton his pants and to put his genitals into his brother Vaso's mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to eyewitness other mistreatments which took place through the use of particular instruments or devices?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If among the instruments for torture can be also counted the device that is used, like an electric prod for cattle, then that was one of them. This was a case in August. I know that it was not in the beginning. Mr. Delic had developed a habit or custom to bring in this device, he would place it against the shoulder or neck of a prisoner and then turn it on. I think he did it most frequently to a person whose nickname was "Sis", who was a policeman before the war in the Konjic municipality. His name was Davor -- probably Kuljanin, his nickname was "Sis". I think he was Kuljanin, Davor Kuljanin, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You were aware of any other particular instrument used for --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I know that certain guards like Kravar, his real name is Enid Spago, he was using intertwined cables, this was about 1 metre in length, several cables that were intertwined, it was like braided together. That was his favourite instrument for treating the prisoners, and also among these instruments was a gas mask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We are not interested in Kravar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I think he is finished about Kravar actually. He is just giving the account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We are concerned with these four accused, not with the other persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In any case, Mr. R, we were saying something about masks. Can you go ahead, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, Zenga had a habit of taking people out, I know that he did this to Jovo Kuljanin, he placed his gas mask on his face, specifically he called out Jovo Kuljanin, he brought him out. When Jovo Kuljanin returned back, he was escorted by Zenga, step by step, and he had this mask on his face, with an air filter which was plugged. His hands were tied behind his back; that is of the victim, of Jovo Kuljanin. Zenga brought Jovo to his place and stood by him until he fainted, and then he took him off. The face of a victim of this gets very ashen type of coloration and only later did his complexion return to normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right, Mr. R. Thank you. Let us go to other topics. Do you know a man by the name Milorad Kuljanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was he also prisoner inside hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was also prisoner in number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you observe an incident concerning Milorad Kuljanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was a witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say approximately when did this incident happen, at least in which month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I can say fairly precisely. Milorad Kuljanin's death occurred on Bajram, which is a Muslim festival, a holiday. I do not know exactly the date when it was in 1992, so I cannot place it particularly, but I know it was on Bajram, because the guards kept saying several days before the Bajram, "if we do not slaughter ten of you for Bajram, we are no good Muslims", and Kravar was the leading one among them, and I apologise to the judge for bringing him up again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. R, can you please give us a detailed account of what happened to Milorad Kuljanin that day? Approximately at what time of the day did this incident happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was morning, could have been 9.00 or 10.00 in the morning, so it was in the morning, I cannot say precisely the hour, because none of us had a watch so we could not say. It was not very early in the morning, it was around 9.00 or 10.00. At that time there was -- the torture of running out in a column to urinate had still not been introduced, so we were still going out in smaller groups, so that this morning I was out with a small group of five or six people and we were relieving ourselves in this canal in front of hangar number 6. While we were still standing there lined up, we heard voices on the railroad tracks, coming from the railroad tracks, and then between this mound and hangar number 6, two guards appeared and at the door, from the door step, they called out Milorad Kuljanin's name, they told him to come out. Milorad came out --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say the names of these two guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The one who called Milorad out and who was the leading person was Esad Macic, whose nickname is Makaron. I do not know the names of the other two guards, because my attention was trained on the person who was actually performing this abhorrent act.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say the names of the other prisoners who were outside with you to urinate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zeljko Cecez, called "Spaniard" and Marinko, I think his last name was Kuljanin he was working the ticket window in the railway station, he was Kuljanin, so there were another two men, but I cannot recall their names right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Macic called Milorad Kuljanin out of the hangar and what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He brought him to us, right there to the canal where --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When you say "he", who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am referring to Macic, to Makaron. He asked him, right there in front of us, which was in our immediate vicinity, "were you in the reserve forces in Mostar?"; that is in the reserve forces of the JNA, this was during the conflict between the army and part of the Mostar population. He said that he was not. The next question asked him by Macic was, "who else from Konjic was there with you in the reserves, because we know you were there". Milorad said that nobody was there, and then Macic ordered him to lie down into this urine which was in the canal, because this urine did not drain through this canal, only if the level rose to a certain level would it drain away, so it was really like a puddle, and the canal was not on an incline so that it would all drain. So he ordered him to lie down facing the ground, and when he lay down and when he was all wet, then he told him to turn around so that he would be lying on his back, so that he would be soaked the other side. Then he again asked him, "who from Konjic was with you in the reserves?" Milorad again repeated that nobody was there. Then he fired from a distance of 20 to 30 centimetres into his face.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You mean "he", who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Macic shot Kuljanin in the face.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: With which kind of weapon did he shoot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what type of weapon it was, it was produced somewhere else, I think it could have belonged to the NATO forces, because I know the weapons produced -- manufactured domestically, because we all had to serve in the army so we knew what was produced by Zastava, so I know it was not one of their weapons, so it must have been from the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How many shots did Macic fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He fired three shots into Milorad Kuljanin's face, into the face and the neck, in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: From where, from which distance could you see this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The distance was such that when these bullets were fired into Milorad Kuljanin's face, the skull sort of burst open, so to speak, and the brains and the blood just splattered on all of us, so it was a very short distance, maybe one step away, so it was very close.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You mean that you personally were reached by this brain and blood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What did the guards do right after this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Immediately the guards ordered us to re-enter the hangar and they closed door behind us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you ever have any chance to see Milorad Kuljanin or his body again after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would just like to mention that about 15 minutes later, the older brother of Macic came, his name is Sead Macic, the younger is Esad Macic, Makaron, the older's nickname was Maca, and he called the five of us out. When we came out, the body of Milorad Kuljanin was no longer there. It had been removed. I do not know where it was taken or by whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You did not see this body any more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, in the sense, no I did not see him again, because it was already removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So you were called outside again after about 15 minutes, all five of you, by the brother of Makaron, and what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He took our names down on a piece of paper, the five of us who were outside, and he said that when we returned in the hangar we should say that we did not see anything. The shot was heard, that is the shots were heard inside number 6, but we should say that we did not see anything, and again he quickly pushed us back inside the hangar and he closed the door. However, additional 15 minutes later --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Let me ask you, before that, let us go back to the very moment of the shots, when you were reached by brain and blood, did you see Milorad Kuljanin falling down, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he fell and the death was immediate, because the skull just opened up and so the exit wounds just burst the skull, so when he fell, he was dead, it was just the last sort of spasms of legs and arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Then you could observe that after that he was motionless?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So let us go ahead then. After the first time you were out then you were called after 15 minutes and then you were saying something else about what happened after 15 more minutes. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The older brother Macic came again and he again called us out, this time by name, from a piece of paper that he had, and he said, "Milorad Kuljanin tried to escape, and he was killed in the process of escaping", so he came back to the hangar just to tell us what we had seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again after a very short time, maybe ten or fifteen minutes, Macic appeared for the third time, he called us out for the third time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You mean Macic or Macic's brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The older brother, and he said that Milorad Kuljanin had tried to snatch away a gun from the guard and that the guard had unintentionally fired and killed Milorad from a close distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So what happened after that? Did you go back into the hangar after this further conversation with Macic's brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Macic again pushed us back in and closed the door behind us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What after that? Did any other incident take place later on the same day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that same day, in the evening, Zeljko Cecez, nicknamed "Spanac", "the Spaniard", was also killed. He was the first on the list compiled by Macic when he took us out, the older brother Macic, when he called us out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Who took Cecez out of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenga took him out. Again, in his inimitable voice, he came in the evening and he called Zeljko Cecez to come out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately at what time of the evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It may have been about 10.00 or 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What happened after Cecez got out of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We heard blows -- let me just mention that nothing in nature can be compared with the sound made by a human being when he is being beaten. It is a sound that cannot be found anywhere else. So we heard the blows hitting the body of Zeljko Cecez, his cries and moans. This may have lasted 25 to 30 minutes, and then the people who were beating Zeljko brought him back to the door of the hangar, and Zenga -- again, I recognised him by his voice, because we had no light -- he said to those people who were right next to the door to throw Zeljko in, and he closed the door. The order was that if anyone tried to assist Zeljko that he would suffer the same fate as he. When the door was closed, if I may?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zeljko probably not knowing himself where he was, as he was probably falling into a coma, he was crying out, "for heavens' sake, is there anyone to help me?" He repeated this several times in the darkness. When the people who were close by had concluded that Zenga and his team had left, they somehow managed to give Zeljko Cecez some water, but soon afterwards, we heard no more cries or moans or anything at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When Cecez was returned into the hangar, could he reach his position inside the hangar by himself or was he brought to his position by somebody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he never reached his position, he was shoved in by Zenga, and his killers, from the door, and maybe only a step or two from the door, his body was found in the morning, he was probably trying to crawl or to move in those last moments of his life, before he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you mean that the following morning when you could see him, you realised he was already dead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was not in his place, he is in between the two inner rows of people, of prisoners, and he was lying in the same position as he was thrown in, his clothes were all torn, his trousers were torn up to above the knees, and the colour of his body was ash grey, as if there was never a drop of blood in that body.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Approximately from which distance could you observe Cecez the following morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The distance was maybe three steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you specifically describe the injuries you could see on this body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One could not see any open wounds on the body because obviously he was beaten with a blunt object, but haematoma could be seen all over his body, from the torn clothes, the trousers, the sweater, they were all torn. One could see the bruises underneath.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How long could you observe the body remaining in the same place in the hangar before he was removed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how long that period could have been, but it was from the beginning of dawn, as soon as it was light enough for us to see the body, until the guards opened the door and ordered the body to be carried out. The guards did not open the door always at the same time, it may have been 6.00 or 7.00, it depended on their will. So it was early morning, from very early morning until the guards opened the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So was that more than one hour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was more than one hour, one and a half, maybe two hours, I really cannot be more precise, but it was more than one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: During this period of time, did the body have any movement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did the body have any sign of life whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that the colour of the body was grey, greyish black, black and blue actually, as if no normal human blood had circulated through that body.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you remember by whom the body was removed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, but one of the prisoners had to carry out that body. It was usually the people sitting close to the door. But I think the order came from the guard Kravar -- I apologise again, I think that morning he was the first to open the door and give orders for the body to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. So Mr. R, let us go to another topic. Do you know a man by the name of Scepo Gotovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he too was a prisoner in hangar number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was he sitting in a position close to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was sitting at the other end in relation to the door and Scepo Gotovac was sitting almost next to the door, so there was quite a bit of distance between the two of us, so if you have the drawing I can show you, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, please. May I ask the usher to provide the witness with the map, which is I think numbered as 182. (Handed). Could you put it on the ELMO, please, so that the witness might show to the court the position of Scepo Gotovac inside the hangar, and maybe mark this position writing with an X, writing "Gotovac" right close to the X.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the drawing, it is already indicated where I used to sit, but Gotovac was here (witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you please write Gotovac near this place? Thank you very much. Did you personally observe an incident concerning Scepo Gotovac? Could you please say, first of all, approximately when this incident happened or at least in which month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact date, but I remember when Gotovac was brought in. He was wearing blue worker's overalls and a cap with a shield. When he was shoved into hangar number 6, and he was shoved in by Mr. Delic, he said, or he asked him, in front of all of us, "why did you kill", I think he said somebody called Jusuf, in 1941 or 1942. Gotovac answered that he had not done that, because at the time he was in a camp, he was not on the spot at all. Then Mr. Delic said to him, "if you had ten lives, you will not survive".

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Then did anything else happen to Mr. Gotovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, according to the established scenario, Zenga would come in the evening, he called out, "Gotovac", he took him out, we heard blows and cries, and some unusual sounds of knocking, and 20 or 25 minutes later, Gotovac was brought back to the door of the hangar, and I think the people next to the door helped him, though he did not have to be moved far to reach his place, if he was still alive at the time. However, in the morning when it dawned, I was rather far away, so I cannot claim anything with precision, but there was something on Gotovac's forehead, nailed on to his forehead, whether it was a cockard, the sign of the Serbian Democratic Party or something else, I cannot tell with precision because it was quite far away from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you observe, even from a distance, Mr. Gotovac sitting there close to the door in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How long could you observe him staying there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As was the case with all the other prisoners who died after beatings overnight, from the moment it became daylight, and until the guards came in and gave orders for the body to be removed, so it could have been an hour and a half or two hours, because I said the guards did not open the doors at exactly the same time every morning, and also none of us had a watch so we could not tell exactly what the time was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you have any chance to get closer to Gotovac before he was removed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not have a chance, I was sitting in my position, and from the distance I could see that there was a sign nailed to his forehead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: From that distance, could you see if Gotovac had any movement or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Gotovac did not move, he lay there in a position that a dead man takes up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right, Mr. R. Do you know a name -- do you know a man by the name Simo Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he too was in hangar number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you personally observe any incident concerning Mr. Simo Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Simo Jovanovic was also taken out several times and beaten before the last time when he passed away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say who called Mr. Jovanovic out of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Zenga called him out, in the usual way, in the evening, when darkness fell, the call would come from the door, Simo Jovanovic went out, and in the morning, the first beating -- after the first beating, he had haematoma all over his body. Then several days later exactly the same occurred. He was called out again by Zenga, Simo was brought to the door of the hangar, and I do not know how he reached his place, but in the morning, when it dawned, he was lying in his place, with a red sweater on him which was quite torn, so you could almost see the whole of his chest naked, which was also black and blue, and his trousers were torn and wet. Whether he was being -- whether any water was poured on him during the beating or during the night, but what I can say is that the trousers were quite wet, because the cloth was of a different colour, part of the trousers was quite dark from the liquid from the dampness. I cannot say whether the top was also wet, because it was red in colour and it does not change colour when it is wet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you hear Zenga saying, Zenga's voice saying anything particular during these occasions, either when he called Jovanovic out or in any way during these incidents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly what the phrase was, but I know that Simo Jovanovic was repeatedly accused of having had machine-gun, weapons, he was asked where they were, who he had given them to, et cetera. I also know that before the war, he was a respected owner of a fish pond, a good man, one might say. Whether his wealth was sold out or not, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When Jovanovic was returned into the hangar, either the first time or any other time, did you recognise any voice saying anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said it was only Zenga's voice who called out these men, and the voice who ordered the prisoners near the door either to move the body of the beaten person to his place, or giving the order not to touch or help, otherwise they would suffer the same fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When Jovanovic was called out the last time and he was returned the last time into the tunnel, did you hear any voice saying anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall such details, I am afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. At this time when he was returned to the hangar the last time, did Jovanovic reach his position in the hangar by himself, or was he brought there by anybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say with certainty, because Jovanovic's position, if I may show you on the drawing, was somewhere here (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you please mark this position with an X and write "Jovanovic" close to the mark?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you in any way observe Jovanovic the following morning after the dawn, after the sunlight came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I could, but it was quite a distance, because he was not quite opposite to me, but he was to one side, but he was on his -- in his place, and I do not know how he managed to reach that place, whether somebody helped him from the door, or he managed himself before dying, I cannot tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you describe the body, any characteristics, any injuries or anything on this body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that he was wearing a knitted woollen sweater, a thick sweater, which was torn, and through the tears one could see the bruises, the black bruises. Also his trousers were quite wet except for at the ends, and I could tell that because the material changes colour when it is wet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What about his face, did you notice anything on his face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I was saying, the face was the colour of earth, grey, the colour of death. He was lying on his back. One could see the whole corpse but especially the head because it was leaning back against the wall of the garage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Turone. I think we will break and come back at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right, your Honour. (4.00 pm) (A short break) (4.30 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Maybe this is the opportunity to announce that the Trial Chamber will be sitting at 11.00 am tomorrow morning, instead of 10.00. (Pause). (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Turone, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. So Mr. R, we were talking about Simo Jovanovic and you just marked his position on that map. My next question is: how long could you observe Jovanovic, or his body, remaining in that same place in the hangar that morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That could have been about an hour or two from the moment of the first light, the break of dawn, that is, until the guards opened the door and ordered the body removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: During this period of time, did the body have any movement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it showed no signs of life.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: By whom was the body removed; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall exactly who it was, but it was some of the prisoners on the orders of guards, I do not know who exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was this the last time you saw the body of Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right, Mr. R. Now, let me ask you, do you know a man by the name Bosko Samoukovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was also a prisoner in number 6, to put it that way. He worked for the rail roads and he had already retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you observe any incident concerning Bosko Samoukovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, virtually all prisoners in the hangar could see that, because Bosko Samoukovic was killed in front of everybody who was in the hangar at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you give us a detailed account of what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was in the period when Bradina was burned down for the second time, to the ground, so that was after 12th July 1992, two or three days after that. Mr. Delic ordered at that time that all prisoners from Bradina be beaten three times during that day, as punishment, and these beatings were administered by either the guards or Delic himself. I know that Zenga entered that day and issued an order, he said, "all people from Bradina get up". For some reason, Bosko Samoukovic did not get up, but remained seated. Zenga came up to him, because he knew he was from Bradina, and said, "why did you not get up?". Bosko got up, and Zenga ordered him to assume this position which was for beating, spread legs, the arms behind the head -- and Zenga at that time was carrying a plank. It was 7 or 8 by 3 to 4 centimetres and it was about 1.2 metres long. At one end was sort of tapered so that he could hold it in his hand. With that sharp edge that was on this piece of wood, he hit Bosko in the kidney area, as Bosko was standing, and in the area of the liver. Bosko fell down, and I think that Delic entered at that moment, and he ordered Bosko to be taken to the infirmary. I know that Brane Gligorevic was sent with him at that time. Brane used to work as a medical technician in Konjic before the war. Shortly thereafter, he came back, maybe after about no longer than 15 minutes, and when he entered the hangar he gave a sign showing that Bosko had already died, and I know also, because next to me, to the right, his son was sitting, and he started crying. In this number 6, there was another son of Bosko's. He also received special treatment by Delic. Twenty times, or however many times Delic would enter number 6, it was always the same procedure. "Samoukovic, get up", so he would have to stand up, turn around and spread legs and put the hands behind his head and Delic would always go through the same treatment. He would hit him several times, kick him in the genitals and this would happen every time that Delic would come into the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: During the beatings of Samoukovic, did Zenga say anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not remember what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: During the beatings done by Mr. Delic, did Delic say anything, as far as you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not remember that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you remember, approximately how long did the beating of Bosko Samoukovic last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That lasted very briefly, only several minutes. But the blows were so hard, and they were delivered with swings, and so -- it was also a man who was already elderly, so the injuries were so serious that Bosko passed away in ten to fifteen minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say, approximately when did this incident happen, at least in which month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This could have been two or three days following 12th July, so 13th -- not really 13th but 14th or 15th July, probably in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right, Mr. R, thank you. Can you tell us now, do you know a man by the name Zeljko Klimenta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was also a prisoner in number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When was the first time you saw Mr. Klimenta in hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw Klimenta for the first time in the hangar when we were transferred from tunnel number 9 to number 6. That was approximately a week after our imprisonment, so this would have been very early in June, so that it would have been June 2nd or 3rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You mean he was in hangar 6 when you arrived, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was already there, he was already in hangar 6 when our group was transferred there, so he was already imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In which conditions was Mr. Klimenta when you arrived in hangar 6 and saw him the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Klimenta was in a very bad shape. I can show it on the drawing, he was in the very corner, opposite the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right, can you mark there with an X there and write Klimenta close to the mark?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did he ever say to you who had beaten him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that on one occasion Delic asked him in a sarcastic way, "so who beat you up?", and Klimenta said, "you did". Zeljko was in very bad shape, I think he had spinal injuries, and we were there together before he was moved to the infirmary, and he was immobile and he was moaning, and I remember very well when Delic asked him, "so who beat you up?", and he said, "you did".

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So Klimenta was brought to the infirmary. Did he ever come back to the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Klimenta may have spent about 40 days in the so-called infirmary and eventually was brought back to number 6. However, those injuries were healed more or less, but he still moved very slowly and with difficulties, he moved his legs with difficulty, and it could appear strange, but Zeljko had more of a freedom of movement than the rest of us prisoners, and maybe it was some kind of crazy courage that he had to move around more around number 6, but from close distance, you could hear the creaking of his bones as he was moving around. The same was with this young man nicknamed Mici. This may sound unbelievable, but that was how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was there a time when any other incident occurred which you could observe or eyewitness in part or in whole concerning Mr. Klimenta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as I said, Klimenta had more of a freedom of movement, maybe because he personally knew all these guards who were in Celebici, or maybe he even assisted them financially so that they would turn a blind eye when he would move around in number 6. I know that one morning, let me backtrack a day, Mr. Emir Kovacic came to the camp and he asked to see Mr. Klimenta and to give him two packs of cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, can you say who is this Mr. Emir Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Emir Kovacic is a man who worked in the health centre in Konjic and he may have visited the camp twice while I was in Celebici. However, whenever Emir Kovacic visited the camp, the next morning somebody would be dead in number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What happened when Emir Kovacic came? Did he come for any reason concerning Klimenta inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He entered number 6 and he was escorted by Mr. Delic, and Kovacic asked to see Klimenta and give him these two packs of cigarettes. I remember Delic then said, "why does he need cigarettes when I am going to kill him tonight?".

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Approximately at what time of the day did this happen, this visit of Emir Kovacic to Mr. Klimenta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that this was in the morning, late morning, maybe it was already day, so 10.00 or 11.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So did anything else happen to Klimenta in the following hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During that night, the following night, I know that the guards called out, "Klimenta", early in the morning, I think it was 4.00 or 5.00 in the morning, so this was the twilight time, neither night nor day, and I know that Miodrag Kujundzic came out with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, who called Klimenta out of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly who called him out at that moment, who the guard was who called Klimenta out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So what happened? He went outside and also Kujundzic went outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and very shortly after he had gone out, a shot was heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you know the reason for which Kujundzic followed Klimenta outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not know the reason, but Kujundzic was distributing food, so he was going to the command building, so he also had more of a freedom of movement than the rest of the prisoners and he was out there with Klimenta that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So you said shortly after Klimenta had gone out, a shot was heard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you ever have a chance to see Klimenta again after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never again, that was the last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did Kujundzic come back to the hangar after the shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you could say it was the next moment, a couple of seconds later, he ran in the door and he was holding his head with his hands and he said, "they killed Zeljko".

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did he say anything more precise about the fate of Klimenta, how it happened, who killed him et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We asked him who killed him and he responded, "it was the guard Padalovic", and that was the only comment that he made.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, may I now tender for admission this Exhibit 182, the map with the marks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can, unless there is any objection to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. R, what role did you observe Mucic having in the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he was the commander in the camp at Celebici, and at Musala in Konjic, so both of them, both camps in Konjic were under his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How do you know that? How do you know that particularly concerning Celebici, of course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How shall I say it? This was general knowledge. If you are looking for small details, I can say that whenever he would come to the camp, which was not often, we had to address him as "Mr. Commander".

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Mucic coming into hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Objection, your Honours. This is a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not think this is a leading question, I just wonder whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No, you can put the question. I do not see what it leads to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mucic coming into hangar 6 during your stay in hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it on two occasions, if we disregard the first time when we were moving to the hangar, so as I said, I did not see him often, but he did come.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Did he always wear a uniform both times when you saw him come in to hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you give us precise details of the two different occasions when Mucic came into hangar 6? Start with the first occasion, whatever you like.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that he once came escorted by Mr. Delic. He entered the hangar and Delic was walking a step behind him to the right on his right side. At that moment, Mr. Mucic was wearing the uniform, but not the same one that we had when we were transferred from the tunnel to number 6. He had a uniform and boots, but he only had a sweat shirt, not a full uniform and he did not wear a hat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was that in any way a camouflage T-shirt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you please give us a precise and detailed account of what happened on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Mucic walked from one prisoner to the next and when he would address any one of us we would have to stand at ready and answer the questions that he asked of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say, approximately when did this occasion take place, I mean at least the month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this was in August, because I believe that the beatings had, so to speak, ebbed in comparison to the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How long did Mr. Mucic remain inside the hangar in this occasion, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was for quite some time, I think it was almost for two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How did he treat prisoners during this couple of hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had to sit in the position I have already described with our legs up against our bodies. Then Mucic would tap somebody on the leg, telling him to get up. He would say, "you", or something to that effect. Then the man would have to get up and to say, "yes, Mr. Commander" and to answer any questions that were put to him. There was no physical beatings, he would just tap a person and this was a sign that he had to get up and stand ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What do you mean, "tap"? Tap with what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With his leg, his shoe or his shin, but it was not a blow to inflict pain, it was just a sign to tell him to get up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did he do that with many prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was quite some time, I do not know whether he spoke to everyone, but to most people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What did he tell them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He mostly asked, "did you have weapons?". I do not know about the others. I remember for example Dusko Bendzo, I remember him because he was the first, and I know he asked him, "how much do the Serbs still owe you for distributing the weapons? How much have you still not collected?", because Dusko Bendzo was a taxi driver before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: At this time, had Dusko Bendzo already received his burns on his legs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so, I think he had, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you remember whether the blisters on Bendzo's leg were visible at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the blisters had dried up, but the scars were still visible, though the blisters were no longer blisters, they were just scars.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When he came close to you, did he also tap you? Did he also talk to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he said, "you".

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What did you do then? Did you stand up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got up, like all the other prisoners, and I stood at attention and said, "yes, Mr. Commander".

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What did he tell you? Did he tell you anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He asked me, "did you have any weapons? Did you have a rifle?"

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What did you answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said, "yes, I did".

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mucic tell you anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he said, "you too wanted a greater Serbia, you too fought for a greater Serbia".

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So this is about the first occasion you said. Do you then remember the other occasion when Mr. Mucic came into hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that he came once and called the Djordjic brothers from the door, Momcilo and Dobroslav and he took them out and they spent some time outside, about 30 minutes, right next to number 6, and Mucic, in an unusually loud voice, spoke to the Djordjic brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you hear what he said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some jokes, it was a chat, but I know that Mr. Mucic said on that occasion, "you are all shit, you and us and there will be no order until the Germans come here, the Schwarber".

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So Mr. R, you said you -- when did you leave Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was transferred from the Celebici camp to another camp in Konjic in the Musala sports hall on 31st August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Who called you out of the hangar when you left Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Delic called me out. He came with a list and he ordered that a box of ammunition be brought for him to sit on, he sat near the door, and he called out the names of 30 prisoners who needed to be transferred from number 6 to Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was there a time when you were released from any kind of detention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, without overstepping the bounds of my testimony, I stayed in Konjic until 5th November, and then I was taken to another camp in Trnovo, which was not registered by any international organisation, not even the International Red Cross, and I was kept there from 5th November until 6th January 1993, waiting to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you finally receive any release document or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not receive absolutely any document, either with any charges against me, nor any release document, nor any other paper except the number under which I was registered by the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. R. Your Honour, my examination-in-chief is finished, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. We will proceed in this way; first counsel for Mr. Landzo, second counsel for Mr. Mucic, third counsel for Mr. Delic and fourth counsel for Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your Honours. May I proceed, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Good afternoon, Mr. R.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My name is John Ackerman. I will have a number of questions to ask you. I am going to try to phrase my questions in such a way that you can answer them easily. In many cases, the only answer that would be required would be a yes or a no. There may be occasions when I will ask you to explain things and then I would expect you to do so, but could you please listen to my questions and only answer the question that I ask you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, only I think that in the case of some questions it is not possible to answer with yes and no, and I hope you will have enough patience and time to hear me out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is what I just suggested to you. If I ask you for an explanation then certainly you may explain, but I think you will find that a number of the questions are very simple and can be answered very simply with a yes or no, okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hate to do this, but I need to do it, as I begin this testimony. I need to ask that the blinds be lowered and that we go into private session so that this witness can come around in front of the model.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us get into closed session. (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Should I go ahead, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. R, you have asked to make an observation about this model and I am going to give you an opportunity to do that. I am going to ask you some questions however and if I fail to give you an opportunity to make your observation please tell me and I will do that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let him start with his observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay, okay start with your observation. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. On this model there is a machine-gun nest that is missing that was in front of number 6 in the latter part of my stay in Celebici, towards the very end, and it was just in front of the door of the hangar, just in front of me now, in front of the hangar, on the garage, on the concrete plateau in front. There was a machine-gun that was facing the door and there was another one in this trench over here above number 6. I do not see that on this model, this machine-gun that was pointing at the door of the hangar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. As a matter of fact, this model is extremely inaccurate in a number of other ways also, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I notice that. I do not know about any other inaccuracies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: For instance, it has the railroad in exactly the wrong place. It shows the railroad coming in from the wrong side of the camp, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean, the wrong side? I do not understand. What do you mean, "from the wrong side"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did not the railroad come into the camp from down here on the end that would be on your left, near this red building, the command building down here on the left-hand side? Is that not where the railroad came in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are thinking over there? If I look at it this way, that is how it was. It entered from this side as it is shown on the model.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know what I am talking about when I refer to the gas station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that the gas station existed and that people were put in manholes there to choke, but I was not put there, so I did not mention them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But my question is, do you recognise, looking at the model, which building on there represents the gas station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, I was not placed in those manholes, but I assume it was this building in front of me. I was not taken to that gas station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That building is also in the wrong place on that model, is it not? That is not where it is actually located.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must repeat again, I was not taken to those manholes, I was not taken to that gas station. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You spent some time in tunnel 9, and it is certainly shown on this model in the wrong place, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is in the right position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know what building I would be referring to if I referred to the command building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is in the wrong place on this model, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is in the right place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right, I would like to, with the usher's assistance, ask that this document be shown to you. I have three copies for the judges and one to be marked and shown to the witness. (Handed). For the Prosecutor, it is a drawing that was furnished to us by your office represented to have been made by this witness. Please put it on the ELMO for me, will you?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D29/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. First of all, my question is: do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was a drawing that was made by you, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately when that drawing was made by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In October or November 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That document shows the railroad coming into the camp right next to the command building, as opposed to what is shown on the model in front of you, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is a difference, but the model is correct, my drawing is not precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That drawing shows the gas station sitting next to and in front of tunnel 9, as opposed to where it appears on the model, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as I was saying, I was not taken to the gas station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One might wonder, if you were not ever taken to the gas station, why you felt it necessary to include it in your drawing. If you did not know anything about it, why did you put it on there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because some 20 or so men who were brought from Brdjani were being choked in the manholes of the gas station and they -- when they appeared, they had almost suffocated, and trying to put all those facts in one place, I put in the gas station, but obviously in the wrong position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you were just guessing and making up the position of the gas station since you knew nothing about it, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew of the men who were taken there and I knew the stories they told, that they were kept there up to nine hours without any air, but as I said, I was not taken there, so I was wrong regarding the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You are an intelligent man, you must understand that I am not asking you about the men who were taken there, I am asking you why you put it on there if you did not know where it was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have already answered your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your answer to my question had to do with men that were taken there. Were you just guessing where it was, were you just trying to make up some evidence, to be helpful, what were you doing when you put it on there not knowing where it was located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because where I was making the statement I was asked to try and reconstruct the places of torture, and at that moment that statement was nothing like the way this testimony is being done, so I tried to put everything down on one piece of paper, but as I said, I was not there at the gas station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Look where you have put the command building. That is not where it appears on the model, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ackerman. I think we should continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you will be more comfortable doing it then. (5.30 pm) (Court adjourned until 11.00 am the following day) 20 21 22 23 24 25
